concepts.name: Non-uniform circular motion
concepts.why: Uniform circular motion holds the angular velocity constant, but a skater who pulls in her arms, a merry-go-round a child starts from rest and a hard disk that slows to a halt when the computer is switched off all change their rate of spin. Motion in a circle at a changing angular velocity is non-uniform circular motion, and it is what the rest of this chapter describes.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by recalling that Chapter 6 discussed only uniform circular motion, names the three everyday cases in which the angular velocity is not constant, and asks in its fourth conceptual question whether a piece of food on a microwave plate is accelerated when the plate starts to spin, turns steadily, and slows to a halt.

concepts.name: Angular acceleration, $\kalpha = \frac{\kdw}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: When the angular velocity changes, the faster the change occurs, the greater the angular acceleration. Angular acceleration is defined as the rate of change of angular velocity, exactly as linear acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, and it is measured in radians per second squared. If the angular velocity increases the angular acceleration is positive, and if it decreases the angular acceleration is negative.
concepts.evidence: The section states the definition as its first new equation, the glossary defines it, and the worked example of the bicycle wheel finds the angular acceleration of a wheel spun up from rest and then the time the brakes need to stop it, where the angular acceleration is negative.

concepts.name: Tangential acceleration, $\kat = \frac{\kdv}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: In circular motion the linear acceleration is tangent to the circle at the point of interest, and so it is called tangential acceleration. It is defined as it was for straight-line motion, as the change in the magnitude of the velocity divided by the time taken, and it tells how fast a point on the rim is speeding up or slowing down along its path.
concepts.evidence: The section names the quantity beside the figure of the semicircle with its tangent arrows, defines it with the same equation one-dimensional kinematics used, and the glossary carries it; the third conceptual question asks the reader to explain why a tangential acceleration changes the magnitude of the velocity but not its direction.

concepts.name: Tangential and centripetal acceleration are perpendicular and independent
concepts.why: Centripetal acceleration changes the direction of the velocity but not its magnitude, and tangential acceleration changes the magnitude but not the direction. The two are perpendicular to each other, so a body in circular motion may have either, both or neither, and each may be considered on its own.
concepts.evidence: The section draws both accelerations on one figure and states that they are perpendicular and independent of one another, and the fourth conceptual question asks which of the two a piece of food on a microwave plate has while the plate starts, turns steadily and stops.

concepts.name: Tangential and angular acceleration, $\kat = \kr\kalpha$
concepts.why: Because the radius is constant in circular motion, the change in the linear velocity is the radius times the change in the angular velocity, and so the tangential acceleration is the radius times the angular acceleration. The greater the angular acceleration, the greater the tangential acceleration, and the smaller the wheel, the smaller the tangential acceleration it gives for the same angular acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the definition of tangential acceleration and $v = r\omega$, prints it in both forms, and the worked example of the motorcycle finds the angular acceleration of its wheels from the linear acceleration of the machine and the radius of the tires.

concepts.name: Rotational quantities and their translational analogs
concepts.why: The angle of rotation, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration are the rotational counterparts of position, velocity and acceleration, and each pair is joined by the radius: the angle is the distance divided by the radius, the angular velocity is the velocity divided by the radius, and the angular acceleration is the tangential acceleration divided by the radius. Recognizing the analogy is what lets everything learned about straight-line motion be carried over to rotation.
concepts.evidence: The section gathers the three pairs and the three relationships into a table of its own, and its first conceptual question asks the reader to name the rotational term analogous to acceleration, force, mass, work, kinetic energy, momentum and impulse.

concepts.name: The rotational kinematic equations, $\kw = \kwo + \kalpha\kt$
concepts.why: Substituting $v = r\omega$ and $a = r\alpha$ into each of the four kinematic equations for straight-line motion makes the radius cancel, leaving four equations in the angle, the angular velocity, the angular acceleration and the time. They describe the motion without any reference to the forces or masses that produce it, and they hold whenever the angular acceleration is constant.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the first of them from $v = v_0 + at$ and then prints all four beside their translational counterparts in a table, and every worked example of the section — the fishing reel spun up, the reel braked to a stop, the freight train's wheels — chooses one of them and solves it.

concepts.name: Average angular velocity, $\kwb = \frac{\kwo + \kw}{2}$
concepts.why: When the angular acceleration is constant, the average angular velocity is halfway between the initial and the final value, just as the average velocity is halfway between the initial and the final velocity in straight-line motion. The angle turned through is then simply the average angular velocity multiplied by the time.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the average angular velocity beside the average velocity and prints $\theta = \bar{\omega}t$ as the first row of its table of kinematic equations; the example of the fly on the microwave plate finds the number of revolutions from the average angular velocity and the cooking time.

concepts.name: Linear quantities from angular ones, $\kx = \kr\theta$
concepts.why: Something spinning in place still carries its rim through a distance, and that distance is the radius times the angle turned through, in radians. In the same way the speed of a point on the rim is the radius times the angular velocity. Radians must always be used in these relationships, and because a radian is dimensionless the product of a length and an angle is a length.
concepts.evidence: The section converts revolutions to radians before every such calculation and warns that this must be done; the fishing reel example finds the speed at which line leaves the reel and the meters of line played out, and the fly on the microwave plate travels eleven meters without going anywhere.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational kinematics problem
concepts.why: A rotational kinematics problem is solved the way a straight-line one is: check that rotation is involved and that forces and masses need not be, identify the unknown, list what is given, choose the equation that contains the unknown and nothing else unknown, substitute with units, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Thinking in terms of the translational analog is useful, because that motion is already familiar.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the six steps as a strategy box of its own and then follows them through three worked examples, and every problem at the end of the section — the gyroscope spun up with a string, the car braking on its tires, the yo-yo unwinding — is solved by choosing among the four equations.

concepts.name: Torque on a point mass, $\ktau = mr^2\kalpha$
concepts.why: A force applied perpendicular to the radius gives a point mass an acceleration $a = F/m$, and since $a = r\alpha$ this is $F = mr\alpha$. Multiplying both sides by the radius turns the left side into the torque, and the result is the rotational analog of Newton's second law for a single point mass, with $mr^2$ standing where the mass stands in $F = ma$.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the figure of a mass on a frictionless table tethered to a pivot, and states that torque is analogous to force, angular acceleration to translational acceleration, and $mr^2$ to mass.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia, $\kI = \sum mr^2$
concepts.why: To rotate anything other than a point mass, the idea of $mr^2$ is extended to a whole body: the moment of inertia is the sum of $mr^2$ over all the point masses of which the body is composed. It plays the part in rotation that mass plays in straight-line motion, it is measured in kilogram meters squared, and because the distance to the axis enters it, a body has a different moment of inertia about every axis.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity, gives the hoop as the one case simple enough to work out by hand, and prints a figure of ten shapes with their moments of inertia that every later section of the chapter sends the reader back to; the glossary carries both rotational inertia and moment of inertia.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia depends on how the mass is distributed
concepts.why: The moment of inertia depends not only on how much mass a body has but on where that mass sits relative to the axis. A merry-go-round full of children is much easier to accelerate when the children stand close to the axis than when they all stand at the rim, although the mass is the same in both cases, because the distance from the axis is squared in every term of the sum.
concepts.evidence: The section states the point directly after defining the moment of inertia, the worked example finds the angular acceleration of a merry-go-round with and without a child sitting on it, and the take-home experiment asks the reader to change the moment of inertia of a cardboard circle and see how much putty is then needed to turn it.

concepts.name: Newton's second law for rotation, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kI\kalpha$
concepts.why: The general relationship among torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration is that the net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. The larger the torque the larger the angular acceleration, and the larger the moment of inertia the smaller it is. The relationship is valid for any torque, applied to any object, about any axis, which makes it the rotational form of Newton's second law.
concepts.evidence: The section states it in both of its forms and says it is very generally applicable, the merry-go-round example uses it twice, and the problems of the section run from a grindstone to Earth's own rotation being slowed by a villain pushing at the equator.

concepts.name: Choosing the moment of inertia for a body and an axis
concepts.why: Calculating a moment of inertia by integration is beyond this text, so the moment of inertia is read from the figure of shapes for the body and the axis at hand: a hoop about its axis, a disk, a rod about its end or about its center, a sphere. Where a system is made of several bodies turning about one axis, the moments of inertia add, since each is a sum of $mr^2$ over the same axis.
concepts.evidence: The section prints the figure of ten shapes for this purpose and says that in all cases but the hoop the reader must consult it; the merry-go-round example adds the child's moment of inertia to the disk's, and later sections of the chapter send the reader back to the same figure for a rod, a sphere and a disk.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational dynamics problem
concepts.why: A problem in rotational dynamics is set up by determining that torque and mass are involved, choosing the system of interest, drawing a free body diagram of the external forces on it, and applying the rotational form of Newton's second law about the point of rotation, with care taken over which moment of inertia belongs to the body and which axis the torques are taken about. As always, the answer is then checked for reasonableness.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the five steps as a strategy box, and the problem about slowing Earth's rotation asks the reader explicitly to show how the steps are followed.

concepts.name: Rotational work, $\text{net}\;\kW = (\text{net}\;\ktau)\theta$
concepts.why: When a net force is kept perpendicular to the radius of a turning disk, the force is parallel to the displacement and the net work is the force times the arc length travelled. Multiplying and dividing by the radius turns the force into a torque and the arc length into an angle, so that the net work is the net torque times the angle turned through. Torque is analogous to force here, and angle to distance.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the expression from the figure of the disk turned by a perpendicular force and says it holds in general although it was derived for a special case; the grindstone example finds the work done through one radian of rotation and confirms that it equals the rotational kinetic energy gained.

concepts.name: Rotational kinetic energy, $\kKErot = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2$
concepts.why: A body has kinetic energy by turning as well as by travelling, and the rotational kinetic energy is half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. The expression is exactly analogous to the translational one, with the moment of inertia standing where the mass stands and the angular velocity where the velocity stands.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity by analogy after deriving the work-energy theorem for rotation, and the glossary carries it; the helicopter example finds that most of a flying helicopter's kinetic energy is in its blades rather than in its motion, and the flywheel bus stores its energy this way.

concepts.name: The work-energy theorem for rotation, $\text{net}\;\kW = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2 - \frac{1}{2}\kI{\kwo}^2$
concepts.why: Substituting the rotational form of Newton's second law into the expression for rotational work, and then using the kinematic relation between the angular velocity and the angle, gives the net work as the change in one half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. Net work changes the kinetic energy of a system, and for a turning body that kinetic energy is rotational.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the theorem step by step and names it, the glossary carries the term, and the grindstone example verifies that the work done by the torque equals the rotational kinetic energy the stone ends with.

concepts.name: A rolling body divides its energy, $\kPEgrav = \kKEtrans + \kKErot$
concepts.why: A body rolling down an incline without slipping converts its gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy of two kinds at once, translational and rotational. The greater its moment of inertia, the more of the energy goes into turning and the less is left to carry it down the slope, which is why a can of thick soup, whose contents turn with the can, loses the race to a can of thin soup, and why a can that slides without rolling wins.
concepts.evidence: The section asks why cans of identical size and mass roll down an incline at different rates, answers it with the figure of the three racing cans, and the example of the solid cylinder shows that the mass and the radius cancel, so that every solid cylinder rolls at the same rate.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational energy problem
concepts.why: Energy problems that involve rotation are solved as other energy problems are: determine that work or energy is involved, choose the system, decide which kinds of work and energy are present, and for a closed system set the initial kinetic and potential energy equal to the final, remembering that the kinetic energy may have both a translational and a rotational part. For an open system the other forms of energy must be accounted for as well.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the seven steps as a strategy box, and the problem about the flywheel bus climbing a hill asks the reader explicitly to show how they are followed.

concepts.name: Angular momentum, $\kL = \kI\kw$
concepts.why: Every rotational phenomenon has a direct translational analog, and angular momentum is the analog of linear momentum: it is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, as linear momentum is the mass times the velocity. It is measured in kilogram meters squared per second. A body with a very large moment of inertia, such as Earth, has an enormous angular momentum, and so does a body turning very fast, such as a centrifuge.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity in its first equation and the glossary carries it; the first worked example calculates the angular momentum of Earth spinning on its axis, and the problems ask for the angular momentum of the Moon, of a skater and of an engine crank.

concepts.name: Torque changes angular momentum, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \frac{\kdLang}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: When you push a merry-go-round, spin a bike wheel or open a door, you exert a torque, and if that torque is greater than the torques opposing it the angular momentum increases. The net torque is the rate at which the angular momentum changes, exactly as the net force is the rate at which linear momentum changes, which makes this the rotational form of Newton's second law.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relationship and calls it very fundamental and broadly applicable; the lazy Susan example finds the angular momentum a partygoer gives a tray by pushing for a seventh of a second, and notes that the angular momentum imparted depends on the torque and the time alone.

concepts.name: Conservation of angular momentum, $\kL = \kLprime$
concepts.why: If the net torque on a system is zero, then its angular momentum does not change: this is the law of conservation of angular momentum, and it stands beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum. It is why Earth keeps on spinning, since only the tides exert any significant retarding torque on it, and why a skater can spin for a long time on ice that opposes her very little.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the law from the relation between torque and angular momentum by setting the net torque to zero, the glossary carries it, and the section's own boxed note places it beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum as another sign of underlying unity in physical laws.

concepts.name: A smaller moment of inertia means a faster spin, $\kI\kw = \kIprime\kwprime$
concepts.why: Because the angular momentum is conserved when no net torque acts, a body that reduces its moment of inertia must increase its angular velocity to keep the product the same. A skater pulling in her arms and her extended leg spins several times faster, an air mass whose radius narrows becomes a tornado, and the cloud of gas and dust that became the Solar System sped up as gravity drew it together.
concepts.evidence: The section writes the conservation law in terms of the moment of inertia beside the two images of the spinning skater, and the worked example finds that a skater spinning at 0.800 rev/s with her arms out reaches 5.16 rev/s when she pulls them in; the tornado, Earth's formation and the merry-go-round problems all turn on the same step.

concepts.name: Work done in pulling in raises the rotational kinetic energy
concepts.why: The skater's angular momentum is unchanged when she pulls in her arms, but her rotational kinetic energy rises sharply, and the increase comes from the work she does pulling her arms inward against the force needed to hold them on their circles. Conserving angular momentum does not conserve rotational kinetic energy, because energy can be added from within the system while the angular momentum cannot.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds the skater's rotational kinetic energy rising from 29.6 J to 191 J while her angular momentum stays the same, the section says the increase comes from work that depletes some of her food energy, and a conceptual question asks the reader to identify the force she exerts on each arm and the distance it moves.

concepts.name: Angular momentum in a collision, $\kL = m\kv r$
concepts.why: Bowling pins fly and spin when the ball reaches them, and cars spin as they collide on ice, so angular momentum has to be carried into the account of a collision. A body moving in a straight line has an angular momentum about a chosen point, since taking it to be a point mass gives $I = mr^2$ and $\omega = v/r$, and the product is the mass times the velocity times the distance to the point. Where the external force acts at the pivot its lever arm is zero, so it exerts no torque and the angular momentum of the system is conserved through the collision.
concepts.evidence: The section works through a disk that strikes and adheres to a nailed stick on a frictionless surface, states that the force at the nail exerts no torque because its lever arm is zero, and uses the conservation of angular momentum to find how fast the two turn afterward.

concepts.name: Solving a collision of extended bodies, $\kwprime = \frac{m\kv r}{\kIprime}$
concepts.why: A collision in which a body is free to rotate is solved by setting the angular momentum before equal to the angular momentum after, both calculated about the same pivot point. The angular momentum before is that of the incoming body treated as a point mass, and the angular momentum after is the combined moment of inertia about the pivot times the angular velocity, where the combined moment of inertia is the sum of the separate ones about that axis.
concepts.evidence: The section carries the disk-and-stick example through in full and the problems repeat it with the disk striking closer to the nail, with the disk already spinning, and with the stick free to travel as well as turn; the twin skaters who lock hands and the person who catches a ball on ice are solved the same way.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy and linear momentum in a rotational collision
concepts.why: Angular momentum may be conserved in a collision while kinetic energy is not, because the collision is inelastic, and linear momentum need not be conserved either, because the force at the pivot may have a component along the incoming body's path. In the disk and stick the kinetic energy falls from 22.5 J to 1.57 J while the linear momentum rises, which the nail explains: the stick pushes back on the nail and the nail pushes forward on the stick.
concepts.evidence: The example calculates the kinetic energy and the linear momentum before and after the collision as well as the angular velocity, and its discussion works out why the momentum afterward is the greater of the two; the conceptual questions ask which quantities are likely to be conserved when a puck strikes a free hockey stick.

concepts.name: The percussion point
concepts.why: Striking the nailed stick at its far end pushes the nail backward and striking it near the nail pushes the nail forward, so there is a point in between at which no force is delivered to the pivot at all. That point is the percussion point. A tennis racquet and a baseball bat have one too, and a ball met there leaves little force and little vibration in the hand, which is what players call the sweet spot.
concepts.evidence: The section reasons from the two extremes of the disk-and-stick collision to the point between them, names it, and draws the three cases for a racquet: struck near the end, struck far down the shaft, and struck at the percussion point.

concepts.name: The right-hand rule for angular velocity and angular momentum
concepts.why: Angular velocity and angular momentum are vectors, and their direction is found by curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the rotation: the thumb then points along the axis of rotation in the direction of both. Because the angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, and the moment of inertia is a positive number, the two point the same way.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rule beside the figure of the turning disk with its arrow along the axis and the drawn right hand, and the glossary carries it; the direction of a torque is found the same way, by curling the fingers in the direction of the force.

concepts.name: A torque changes angular momentum in its own direction
concepts.why: The net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so the change in angular momentum points the way the torque points. When the torque is perpendicular to the angular momentum already there, the two add head to tail to give a new angular momentum of the same size pointing in a new direction, and the axis of rotation moves perpendicular to the forces applied rather than the way they push.
concepts.evidence: The section applies the rule to a bicycle wheel with handles that a person tries to tip, draws the vector sum of the angular momentum and its change, and notes that the wheel moves toward the person instead of the way she pushes it.

concepts.name: Gyroscopic precession
concepts.why: The weight of a spinning gyroscope and the force from its stand create a horizontal torque, always perpendicular to the angular momentum, so the direction of the angular momentum changes while its magnitude does not and the gyroscope precesses about a vertical axis instead of falling over. A gyroscope that is not spinning simply acquires angular momentum in the direction of the torque and falls. Earth precesses in the same way, once in about 26,000 years, under the torque of the Sun and the Moon on its nonspherical shape.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the two forces on a spinning gyroscope and the vector diagram of the angular momentum turning, says that Earth's axis points at Polaris and slowly precesses, and the section's one problem finds the torque that produces that precession.
